evidence.label: Strong diffeomorphic approximation in three dimensions for 1≤p≤2
Strong diffeomorphic approximation in three dimensions for p>2

headline: Claims to solve the Ball–Evans problem in 3D: every Sobolev homeomorphism is a strong limit of smooth diffeomorphisms.
scope: Sobolev homeomorphisms between any two bounded connected open sets in ℝ³, for every exponent 1 ≤ p < ∞. Two companion papers split the range of p.
plain: Engineers model a squashed solid as a map that sends each point to its new place. The map must be one-to-one, so no two bits of material overlap. Mathematicians asked whether such a rough map can be approached by smooth one-to-one maps, with the derivatives also close. This was known in the plane and false in dimension four and up for some exponents. Two papers claim a yes in three dimensions, for every finite exponent.
doesNot: This does not claim the inverse maps converge in a Sobolev sense, and it says nothing about dimensions four and up. It has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: John Ball, who attributed the question to Lawrence Evans
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle a well-known problem from nonlinear elasticity in the physical dimension three, for every finite exponent.

explanation:
Start with a ball of rubber of radius 1. Move each point x to a point in the same direction, at distance √r, where r is the old distance from the centre. A point at r = 0.25 moves out to 0.5. A point at r = 0.01 moves out to 0.1. This map is one-to-one and fills the same ball. Near the centre it stretches hard. At r = 0.01 it stretches lengths around the centre by 10 and lengths away from it by 5. At r = 0.25 these numbers are 2 and 1. So the map has no derivative at the centre itself. Still, the total of the squared stretch over the ball is finite: it is 4.5π, about 14.14.

Maps like this are Sobolev homeomorphisms. A homeomorphism is a one-to-one, onto map that is continuous both ways. It is in W^{1,p} if its values and its weak derivative, a derivative defined by averages, have finite p-th power totals. Engineers use such maps for elastic solids. One-to-one means no two pieces of material overlap.

The question is whether smooth maps can copy this one. A diffeomorphism is a smooth one-to-one map with a smooth inverse. We want diffeomorphisms onto the same target whose values and derivatives get close in the p-th power sense. Ball posed this and credited the question to Evans[3]. Smoothing alone is easy, but the usual averaging, called convolution, can break one-to-one[4]. For example, average the identity map with the half-turn x ↦ −x. Both are one-to-one, but the average sends every point to 0.

In the plane, Iwaniec, Kovalev and Onninen solved the problem for p > 1[5]. Hencl and Pratelli handled p = 1[6]. In dimension four and up, Campbell, Hencl and Tengvall built counterexamples for some small p[7]. Dimension three stayed open.

The first paper claims the answer is yes in three dimensions for 1 ≤ p ≤ 2[1]. The second paper claims yes for every finite p > 2[2]. Neither paper assumes anything about the boundary of either set[8]. The main obstacle is that three-dimensional topology gives one-to-one replacements but no bound on their derivatives[9]. So each paper must measure energy directly. The first paper builds a one-to-one map that stretches only by bounded amounts and is close in energy. It then smooths that map with fine control[10]. The papers do not claim the inverse maps converge in the Sobolev sense[11].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. Both proofs are long and technical. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: A major claim if the proofs hold: it would settle a well-known problem in three dimensions. The proofs are long, there is no Lean check, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A one-to-one, onto map that is continuous, with a continuous inverse.
A smooth one-to-one, onto map whose inverse is also smooth.
A derivative defined through averages, so it can exist for maps with corners or spikes.
The maps whose values and weak derivatives have finite p-th power totals over the domain.
Getting close in both values and derivatives, measured by p-th power totals.
Smoothing a map by replacing each value with a weighted average of nearby values.
